title: SYSK Selects: The Wind Cries Typhoid Mary
summary: Selects episode (rerun) of the original 2011 Stuff You Should Know episode "The Wind Cries Typhoid Mary." Josh introduces it as a favorite and opens with late-19th-century New York horse manure and the Department of Sanitation's White Wings cleaners. The hosts then cover typhoid fever and its history, and the case of Mary Mallon: the Irish-born cook identified as a healthy carrier by sanitation engineer George Soper in Oyster Bay in 1906. They discuss her forced quarantine on North Brother Island, her court case, her release and laundry job, and her return to cooking at Sloane Hospital, which led to more infections and deaths. They close with reflections on civil liberties versus public health and a listener mail correction about the Moon episode.

entities.name: Nova: The Most Dangerous Woman in America

segments.title: Selects intro and choice of episode
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Saturday Selects episode, choosing The Wind Cries Typhoid Mary from October 2011 because he likes it and the title.

segments.title: Horse manure in 19th-century New York
segments.summary: The hosts estimate the daily horse manure on New York streets from about 200,000 horses, and describe the lack of street cleaning. The city's Department of Health and the White Wings cleaners were created in response, and the phrase cleanliness is next to godliness is linked to that effort.

segments.title: Civil liberties and typhoid fever
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Health Department's broad powers, including forced inoculation and quarantine. They explain that germ theory was new and the public had not been told about it. They then describe typhoid fever, its symptoms, its famous victims, and its death rate before antibiotics.

segments.title: Oyster Bay outbreak and George Soper
segments.summary: In summer 1906 typhoid broke out at the Thompson family's house in Oyster Bay. Sanitation engineer George Soper was hired to investigate. After interviewing household members, he learned that former cook Mary Mallon had worked for several families where outbreaks occurred.

segments.title: Healthy carrier theory and Mary Mallon's background
segments.summary: The hosts explain the healthy carrier concept: a person whose immune system keeps the bacteria alive without illness. Soper believed Mallon was one. They describe her Irish background, her career as a cook, and her refusal to give samples, which the hosts say may have included a carving fork.

segments.title: Mallon's forced isolation on North Brother Island
segments.summary: Commissioner Herman Biggs sent officials to take Mallon, who hid for hours before being removed. She was held at a quarantine hospital on North Brother Island, refused to stop cooking, and was isolated there. The hosts describe the island's reputation and treatment, including forced medication.

segments.title: Court case, press coverage, and the name Typhoid Mary
segments.summary: Mallon's private lab tests did not match the Health Department's results. She went to New York Supreme Court, which ruled against her and sent her back to the island. Newspapers, including Hearst's, covered the case, and she became known as Typhoid Mary.

segments.title: Release, laundry job, and return to cooking
segments.summary: After three years, a new health commissioner released Mallon and offered her a laundry job, which she disliked. She later worked under an assumed name as a cook at Sloane Hospital, where Soper identified her after doctors and nurses fell ill. She was blamed for about 50 cases and three deaths. The hosts note she had been offered alternatives she refused.

segments.title: Legacy and debate over civil liberties
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether Mallon was a bad person and the lasting debate over civil rights and public health. They mention the Nova documentary and related resources, including the Black Death episode on quarantine.

segments.title: Listener mail: Moon corrections
segments.summary: A listener named Chris B corrects the Moon episode. The Moon does rotate, though it is tidally locked; it has a far side, not a permanently dark side; and tides come mainly from the Moon's horizontal gravity differential, not from pulling water up.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and give ways to send corrections and find more information.
